Default (self-host / unconfigured): LOCAL DISK at <app>/uploads/, served from /uploads/<path> on the app's own origin.

Managed platform: S3 + CloudFront on an ISOLATED, cookieless origin - the platform media CDN domain (benmore.ai serves media.benmoreusercontent.com, and usercontent.benmore.ai URLs still resolve) - with a per-app key prefix. This is the fleet default on benmore.ai - uploads return CDN URLs automatically, no per-app config. Serving user content off a separate origin means a malicious file can't touch app sessions; CloudFront also forces nosniff + a script-killing CSP on every object.

Per-app override: set S3_BUCKET (+ S3_REGION/S3_KEY/S3_SECRET or an IAM role, S3_ENDPOINT for R2/MinIO) to use your own bucket. Takes precedence over the platform default. On the hosted platform S3_ENDPOINT must resolve to a public address (checked at connect time).

Tenant isolation: an app can only write under its own prefix (server-derived), and can only sign/serve its own private files (serve_file clamps to the calling app). Public files are unguessable-URL capability on a shared cache (no listing exposed).

dev_instance_prefix: each instance has its own prefix - prod `<sub>`, the dev instance `<sub>-dev` (URLs `https://<media CDN>/private/<sub>-dev/uploads/...`). New uploads on dev land under `<sub>-dev`, and delete_upload on dev accepts only `<sub>-dev` references (a production URL fails before any storage call), so a dev flow cannot delete production's files. Dev still SERVES production's references - serve_file, bm.signedUrl and transcribe accept a `<sub>` URL on dev - so rows copied by `refresh-dev --with-data` and older dev uploads stored under `<sub>` keep working; those, being under `<sub>`, cannot be deleted from dev. A logical `uploads/private/...` path resolves to the instance's own prefix. Prod never serves `<sub>-dev` objects. Deleting the app removes both prefixes. The platform's media signer enforces this per instance: every request carries a proof under the instance's own server secret.

signed_link_lifetime: a signed link to a private file is a bearer capability for that one object, capped at 6 hours. A `<video>`/`<audio>` element keeps range-requesting the URL it was redirected to for as long as it plays, so a short link would stall long playback with a CDN 403. serve_file signs audio/video (mp4, m4v, mov, webm, ogv, mkv, 3gp, mp3, m4a, aac, wav, flac, ogg, oga, opus, weba) for 4 hours and everything else for 2 minutes; set another lifetime with the literal `with: { expires_in: 2h }` (whole seconds or a duration, 1s to 6h; a template is refused, so a request cannot choose it). bm.signedUrl defaults to 300 seconds, and audio/video to the same 4 hours when you pass no ttlSeconds; GET /api/_signed_url without expires_in gives 1 hour, or 4 hours for audio/video. `expires_in` (what bm.signedUrl sends ttlSeconds as) is read like serve_file's: whole seconds (`300`) or a duration (`30s`, `90m`, `2h`), at least 1s; a duration's fraction of a second is dropped, and more than 6 hours gives 6 hours. A value that cannot be read or is under one second (`abc`, `0`, `-5`, `1.5`, `500ms`) answers 400 `invalid_expires_in` with no link: a link never outlives the lifetime asked for (api({at:'signed-urls'}) → lifetime). HLS/DASH playlists are not covered: their segments are separate objects.

Signing on the hosted platform: the app holds no signing key. The platform signs each private URL (serve_file, bm.signedUrl, transcribe downloads) for the app's own prefix only, for at most 6 hours. If the platform signer is unreachable the request fails with 500 `media signing unavailable`; it never falls back to an unsigned or locally signed URL. Self-hosted and `benmore host` sign with the key in their own environment.
